paragraphs.heading: What eusociality means
paragraphs.text: Eusociality is the most highly organized form of social life. It is defined by three features. Adults care for young together, including young that are not their own. Several adult generations live side by side in one colony. And the members are split into those that breed and those that do not, forming specialized groups that are sometimes called castes.

paragraphs.heading: Who does what
paragraphs.text: In a colony, queens and reproductive males are the only ones that breed. Soldiers and workers cooperate to keep the colony a good place for raising the young. Queens hold this arrangement together with several chemical signals called queen pheromones, and they may also keep control by fighting or by eating eggs that other females lay. A colony can be pictured as a superorganism: each caste is like one tissue or cell type in a single body, doing one job for the whole and unable to survive alone outside the colony.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is found
paragraphs.text: Eusociality has arisen among insects, crustaceans, trematodes and mammals. It is commonest in the Hymenoptera, the group of ants, bees and wasps, and in termites. Every ant species is eusocial, while only a moderate share of bee and wasp species are. Among insects it has evolved several separate times, including thrips, aphids and beetles. Other examples include a shrimp called Synalpheus regalis and two rodents, the Damaraland mole-rat and the naked mole-rat, and Wilson and others have claimed that humans show a weak form of it.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: Suzanne Batra coined the word eusocial in 1966 for the nesting behaviour of Halictid bees. She saw that the bees, males and females alike, each took on at least one job in the colony, such as digging burrows, building cells or laying eggs. Cooperation was essential, since what one group did strongly affected the work of another. In 1971 Wilson widened the idea to other social insects such as ants, wasps and termites, and it was later found in mole-rats, which are chordates.

paragraphs.heading: The point of no return
paragraphs.text: Researchers do not all agree on how strict the definition should be. Crespi and Yanega argued for a point of no return: each individual is locked into one behavioural group, usually before it can breed, and cannot switch later. That leaves members truly dependent on each other to survive and reproduce. In many insects this has reshaped the bodies of the workers, which are sterile and support the breeding caste. Such a strict definition would rule out most claimed cases of eusociality in mammals.

paragraphs.heading: A continuum of helping
paragraphs.text: Other researchers argue that cooperative breeding and eusociality are not separate categories but points along one continuum. What mainly differs between these societies is how lifetime breeding success is shared out among group members. Both vertebrate and invertebrate species that breed cooperatively can be placed on one common scale of that variation. On this view, labels like primitive and advanced eusociality should be dropped, and every case of helping to care for related young can be explained by one theory, such as Hamilton's rule.

paragraphs.heading: Division of labour in a wasp nest
paragraphs.text: The social wasp Polistes versicolor shows how sharp the split of work can be. Dominant females build new cells and lay eggs, while subordinate females mostly feed the larvae and forage. Subordinates do 81.4% of all the foraging, against 18.6% for dominants. Chemical signals can help with work too: workers of the Australian stingless bee Tetragonula carbonaria mark food with a pheromone so that nestmates can find it.
